questions.question: Define an illegal connection, describe the forms it takes, and set out the layered reasons people make them.
questions.expected_answer: An illegal connection, known as izinyoka, is a connection to the electricity network that the utility has not installed, metered or approved, so electricity flows unmeasured and unpaid through wiring no qualified person has installed or inspected. Forms include a cable clamped onto bare overhead conductors or streetlight terminals, a cable run from a legal house's meter box to unconnected houses, a bypassed or tampered prepaid meter, and a connection to a forced-open substation or kiosk. People make them because of absence, where settlements on unproclaimed or disputed land have no legal supply; cost, where connection fees and unit prices are beyond households on grants; time, where electrification waiting lists run for years; normalisation, where whole streets are connected and local connectors operate as businesses; and sometimes politics, where connections and protests are used to force attention.

questions.question: Explain why illegal connections are so dangerous, describe the three main hazards, and identify who is harmed beyond the user.
questions.expected_answer: A legal supply has a meter, an earth, a main circuit breaker and earth-leakage protection that cut current the instant a fault appears; an illegal connection has none, so every fault runs to completion. Shock and electrocution occur when exposed taped joints, cables at head height across roads, cables in puddles or buried cables cut during digging deliver the full supply with nothing to interrupt it, killing children and the workers who remove connections. Fire occurs when thin cable carrying a heater's current heats like an element, melting insulation and igniting tape in shacks that spread fire to neighbours in minutes. Overload occurs when a transformer sized for fifty houses carries hundreds of shacks with heaters, overheats and fails, cutting legal customers off for days and draining repair budgets. Beyond the user, streetlights go dark, legal households pay for neighbours' use or are disconnected for tampering, the utility loses billions and raises tariffs, workers are threatened, and the connected household cannot report the hazard it depends on.

questions.question: Identify the five values in tension in the ethics of illegal connections, give the main arguments for and against the household, and describe the balanced position and the practical response that follows from it.
questions.expected_answer: The values are need, the right to basic energy for a dignified life; law and property, that unpaid taking is theft regardless of need; fairness, which cuts both ways between those who wait years unserved and paying customers who subsidise non-payers and lose supply; safety, that one's need does not justify endangering others' children; and responsibility, over who must fix the situation among household, connector, municipality, utility and state. For the household, the Constitution promises progressive access to basic services, electricity is essential for safety, schooling and health, the household did not choose to be unserviced, and condemnation without an alternative is empty. Against, theft harms everyone including other poor households, the danger falls on non-consenting neighbours, connectors profit from desperation, and tolerance undermines the systems that could deliver legal supply. The balanced position holds that the need is real, the connection is still wrong because of the danger to others, the greater fault lies with those who left the settlement unserved, and the response must both remove dangerous connections and deliver safe legal supply quickly through pole-mounted ready boards, free basic allocations and prepaid meters, which has reduced illegal connections where done.
